title: Knowledge taught together moves together
statement: What was taught together tends to be known or missing together, so in a course with few prerequisites, sample a diagnostic by teaching unit rather than testing every component.
example: At 3 items for each of 400-600+ components, testing every component of an AP course would take 1,200-1,800 items, roughly 10-15 hours.
detail: The diagnostic BrainLift argues that components taught in the same unit and the same week have correlated mastery, not because they depend on each other but because the causes of knowing them are shared, so two failed items from one unit should lower the estimate for the whole unit (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback3/WF - Assessment  Feedback Brain - 260624-200115.md`). It calls this instructional clustering and leans on it in subjects with many components and sparse prerequisite structure, where prerequisite chains cannot carry the inference. A well-decomposed AP course might hold 400-600+ components, and at 3 items each that is 1,200-1,800 items, roughly 10-15 hours of testing.
against: This is the BrainLift's statistical argument; nothing in the evidence measures how strongly mastery moves together within a unit.

evidence.quote: KCs taught in the same unit, by the same teacher, in the same week, will be correlated in their mastery status — not because the KCs are logically related, but because the *causes* of knowing or not knowing them are shared.
instructional clustering, which exploits shared exposure history rather than logical dependencies
A well-decomposed AP course might contain 400-600+ knowledge components. At 3 items per KC (a bare minimum for defensible inference), that's 1,200-1,800 items — roughly 10-15 hours of testing.
